text: This did not come from nowhere.
The University of Chicago was the home of a famous school of urban sociology.
Robert Park and Ernest Burgess borrowed words from plant biology to describe city neighborhoods.
They wrote about invasion and succession, as if a Black family moving onto a block were a species pushing out another.
The language made segregation sound like a law of nature instead of a choice people made.
Hoyt took that frame and gave it a dollar sign.
A neighborhood, he argued, lost value the moment certain people arrived.
He never quite asked the obvious question.
Did the value fall because Black families moved in, or because white owners and white banks decided it should, and pulled their money out to make it true.
He measured the wound and called it weather.
So far this was a theory in a book.
Then the federal government hired the man who wrote it.
In 1934 Congress created the Federal Housing Administration to insure home loans and pull the country out of the Depression.
It needed to decide which mortgages were safe to back.
Homer Hoyt became its chief land economist.
Working beside him was Frederick Babcock, the appraiser who built the agency's underwriting system and who taught that property values fell when the wrong races moved in.
